title: Offshore construct: sea forts, reclaimed land, and causeway routing
summary: Extend the construct op to place structures IN the sea -- reclaiming land under them and routing a causeway instead of a road -- so sea forts can guard the ocean approaches, with a larger paired fort as the hangar/launch site and another nearby as the Directorate's NERV-analog HQ.
description:
Requested directly after the bunker vertical slice landed: 'You need a plan for how to add new buildings to the ocean too as I want the sea forts to protect the ocean approaches but also a larger pair of sea forts will be the hanger/launch location and another one nearby will be the HQ for our version of NERV.' This is the plan, written out rather than half-built alongside everything else that same session (terrain benching, water-avoidance, the CLI) -- it touches three genuinely separate pieces of machinery and deserves its own pass rather than being rushed in as a fourth thing on top of an already-large change.

**What has to change, concretely:**

1. **Anchor-in-sea detection.** apply_construct currently never asks whether its anchor is on land or water. The check is cheap (`world.sea.sea_geom.contains(anchor_point)`, same geometry returnToSea already touches) but it forks everything downstream -- an offshore anchor needs land reclaimed under it before any of the existing building/footprint logic makes sense.

2. **Reclamation is returnToSea's exact inverse.** returnToSea (ops/demolish.py) unions a polygon INTO world.sea. Reclaiming for an offshore construct is `sea_geom.difference(footprint.buffer(margin))` -- the same SeaResult-replace pattern, opposite operation. This is why returnToSea was worth generalizing when it was built rather than one-offing it for the airport: the reclaim half was always going to want the identical mechanism.

3. **New land needs its own elevation baseline, not benching.** The existing terrain-bench (construct.py, 'build up to the max sampled elevation') doesn't apply to open water -- there is no real land elevation to sample toward. A reclaimed island needs a flat TerrainEdit at a fixed freeboard above sea level instead (a few metres, matching how a real artificial island or caisson platform sits above the waterline), plus probably a seawall/revetment ring at the edge for the render to read as reclaimed land and not a rendering error -- design/map-generation.md's own `reclaim` op (already named in ops/log.py's KNOWN_OPS, never implemented) is exactly this, and offshore construct should probably just call it rather than duplicating the logic.

4. **Causeway routing is real new router capability, not a small extension.** router.py's state lattice currently treats terrain as the only cost surface and has no notion of water at all -- a routing grid built over sea would see NaN/obstacle everywhere offshore (build_routing_grid samples DEM, and GSI has no meaningful elevation for open water). The original design plan (before the vertical slice narrowed scope) called for water as a SPAN cost -- `BRIDGE_FIXED + span_m * BRIDGE_PER_M`, applied per bridge segment rather than per cell, with the result tagged `bridge=yes` so it renders on top of what it crosses (matching how the existing bridge z-order pass already works for ordinary road bridges). Implementing this properly means the router needs a genuine second mode -- 'is this cell sea, and if so what does crossing it cost' -- not a patch on the existing land-only cost function. This is the single largest piece of new work here and should get the same adversarial-testing treatment (determinism, corridor containment, a real span-cost regression test) the land router got.

5. **Multiple, related structures.** The ask is specifically for a SET: several smaller forts guarding the approaches, a larger PAIR functioning together as hangar/launch, and one more nearby as HQ. Nothing about applying construct N times in a row is new, but the pair likely wants an inter-fort causeway (not just each-to-mainland), which is the same causeway router applied between two offshore anchors instead of one offshore anchor and the mainland network -- worth checking the router's goal-mask logic generalizes to 'nearest OTHER offshore anchor' as cleanly as it currently does to 'nearest mainland road'.

**Suggested build order**, each independently testable: (a) anchor-in-sea detection + reclaim-as-returnToSea's-inverse, tested by placing a small platform in open water with no causeway requirement yet, confirming new land renders correctly and the coastline stroke updates; (b) the causeway span-cost router mode, tested in isolation against a synthetic sea mask exactly like router.py's existing land tests use synthetic elevation; (c) wire the two together for a single offshore construct; (d) the multi-fort case with an inter-fort causeway.

Worldbuilding note, not a design decision: 'our version of NERV' confirms the tokusatsu/mecha-anime register the Directorate/Frame framing was already implying -- useful context for naming and flavor text on these structures, not something to resolve here.
sourceContext: Follow-up feedback on the bunker vertical slice (tools/city-map/), same session that added terrain benching and water-avoidance to construct.py after the user caught the bunker sitting on a river.
openSubQuestions: Exact freeboard elevation for reclaimed land above sea level -- a fixed constant, a style/frame setting, or a per-op payload field?

Does the causeway router share router.py's RoutingGrid/state-lattice machinery with a new cost mode, or does open water crossing want its own simpler module (a sea crossing is mostly just 'shortest reasonable span between two points', without the curvature/switchback concerns that drove the land router's whole design)?
Seawall/revetment ring around reclaimed land: a new template part kind, or generated automatically by the reclaim op itself?

How many approach forts, and where -- this is a real design question (which sea lanes matter, how they relate to Kobe Airport's former location now that it's reclaimed by the sea) for the user, not something to default silently.
resolution: Phase (a) built 2026-08-24 (anchor-in-sea detection + reclaim-as-returnToSea's-inverse + flat freeboard elevation instead of benching), directly in apply_construct rather than as a separate reclaim op -- construct.py already had every other piece of machinery this needed (footprint conflict checking, TerrainEdit creation, the World/SeaResult replace pattern already proven by demolish.py's returnToSea), so forking on is_offshore inside the existing function was less duplication than routing through ops/log.py's still-unimplemented reclaim op kind. 15 new tests (test_construct.py::TestOffshoreConstruct), plus a real-data check placing a test platform in the now-open water where Port Island used to be (both islands were removed the same session -- see data/map/operations/kurose.json op-0003/op-0004). Resolved the freeboard/seawall sub-questions pragmatically: freeboardM defaults to 4.0m, overridable per-op; no new template-part kind or generated seawall geometry was needed at all -- the render pipeline's existing hole-aware sea fill (proven by TestSeaHoleAware for real islands) already draws a correct coastline stroke around ANY hole in world.sea, including a freshly reclaimed one, for free. Router-architecture sub-question still open. Phases (b) causeway span-cost routing, (c) wiring a routed causeway into offshore construct, and (d) the multi-fort/inter-fort-causeway case are NOT built -- an offshore construct today gets new land and a building but no access at all (report.road_reason says so explicitly). Site selection for the actual sea forts (count, roles, exact placement) is also still open -- construct.py can build them the moment real anchors are chosen.
